'''''Dianthus armeria''''', the '''Deptford pink''' or '''grass pink''',<ref name=ROM>Dickinson, T.; Metsger, D.; Bull, J.; & Dickinson, R. (2004) ROM Field Guide to Wildflowers of Ontario. Toronto:Royal Ontario Museum, p. 234.</ref> is a species of ''[[Dianthus]]'' ("pink") native to most of [[Europe]], from [[Portugal]] north to southern [[Scotland]] and southern [[Finland]], and east to [[Ukraine]] and the [[Caucasus]].<ref name=fe>Flora Europaea: [http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Dianthus&SPECIES_XREF=armeria&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= ''Dianthus armeria'']</ref><ref name=dvf>Den Virtuella Floran: [http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/caryophylla/diant/dianarm.html ''Dianthus armeria'' (in Swedish, with maps)]</ref><ref name=blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}</ref> It is naturalised in [[North America]].<ref name=ROM/>

==Description==
[[File:(MHNT) Dianthus armeria - Plant habit.jpg|alt=Deptford Pink (Dianthus armeria) in flower|thumb|Deptford pink (''Dianthus armeria'')]]
''Dianthus armeria'' is an annual or biennial plant which grows to about {{convert|60|cm|ft}} tall and has a very slender appearance. It has widely spaced, paired leaves, and above these it branches rather sparingly.<ref name = IWF>{{cite web | url = https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/weeds/plants/deptford_pink.htm | title = Deptford Pink ''Dianthus armeria'' | accessdate = 24 March 2020 | publisher = Illinois Wild Flowers}}</ref> At the ends of the stems there are short-stalked or stalkless clusters of deep-pink flowers that are surrounded by erect, hairy, leaf-like bracts. These can also be located laterally. Each flower is {{convert|8|to|13|mm|in}} in diameter and has 5 [[Glossary of leaf morphology#lanceolate|lanceolate]] petals, each with irregular serrated edges and small white spotting on the upper surface.<ref name = BSBI>{{cite web | url = https://bsbi.org/wp-content/uploads/dlm_uploads/Dianthus_armeria_species_account.pdf | title = ''Dianthus armeria'' L. | accessdate = 24 March 2020 | publisher = Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland}}</ref> The leaves are hairy, dark green in colour and slim in shape.<ref name = Plantlife>{{cite web | url = https://www.plantlife.org.uk/uk/discover-wild-plants-nature/plant-fungi-species/deptford-pink | title = Deptford Pink ''Dianthus armeria'' | accessdate = 24 March 2020 | publisher = Plantlife}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Dianthus armeria'' is native to Europe, where it is widespread as far north as 60°N in Scandinavia, extending eastwards to Armenia and the [[Caucasus]], and as far south as Spain and Sicily. It has been introduced to North America, where it is now naturalised and is widespread as an [[invasive species]].<ref name = BSBI/> In Britain it is now extirpated as a native species from Scotland and is known from a few dozen sites in England and 4-5 sites in Wales, including a nature reserve in [[Flintshire]], a quarry near [[Pontypridd]] in [[Rhondda Cynon Taf]], near a reservoir in the vicinity of [[Port Talbot]] and along a farm track on a site near [[Llanelli]].<ref name = BBC>{{cite news | url = https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-wales-10986418 | title = Deptford Pink's Flintshire site sees 14-fold increase | work = BBC News | date = 30 August 2010 | accessdate = 24 March 2020 }}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
''Dianthus armeria'' is a species of open and periodically disturbed sites. It is normally an annual but can be biennial or a short-lived perennial. New leaf rosettes form at the base of old plants from buds located on their roots, demonstrating that this species is in fact a short-lived perennial and has a life-span of less than two and a half years.<ref name = BSBI/> It flowers from July to September.<ref name = Plantlife/> Its flowers are scentless and do not appear to be insect pollinated often, with self-pollination the norm. Each plant gradually releases around 400 seeds from their pods; however, some plants may hold a small fraction of the seeds they produce over winter.<ref name = BSBI/> It closes its blooms in the late afternoons.<ref name = Plantlife/>

==Cultivation and uses==
[[File:Dianthus_armeria_seeds.jpg|thumb|left|Seeds of ''Dianthus armeria'']]
It is widely grown as an [[ornamental plant]] in gardens. Populations have been introduced to and have become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in [[New Zealand]] and much of [[North America]].<ref name = USDA>{{cite web | url = http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=DIAR | title = ''Dianthus armeria'' L. Deptford pink | access-date = 24 March 2020 | publisher = USDA}}</ref>

==Name==
The name Deptford pink was coined in the 17th century by naturalist Thomas Johnson, who described a pink flower growing in [[Deptford]] in southeast London. However, it is very likely that Johnson was actually describing the related [[Dianthus deltoides|maiden pink]], and it is unlikely that this species has grown in the area it is named after since the city of London was built.<ref name = Wildlife>{{cite web | url = https://www.wildlifetrusts.org/wildlife-explorer/wildflowers/deptford-pink | title = Deptford Pink | accessdate = 24 March 2020 | publisher = The Wildlife Trusts}}</ref>
